speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING IN QUEBEC CITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I indicated to the house on Friday that I would make a statement on motions on the recent federal-provincial conference held in Quebec city. Owing to the importance of the matters dealt with at this conference, I should apologize for the fact that the statement will be, I think, somewhat longer than is normally desirable in statements on motions; but I hope in this particular situation that will be understood and accepted. Even then it will not be possible for me to deal with all the matters discussed at Quebec, or perhaps fully deal with the three or four that I propose to mention.
The first matter which we discussed there, which is of immediate importance and interest to the house and indeed is before the house now, was the Canada pension plan. That matter of a contributory, nation-wide pension plan had been discussed at the conference held last November, and this was a continuation of the discussion we had at that time in the light of developments which had occurred in the meantime. I think it can be said that in the light of the discussion at Quebec the provincial and federal viewpoints have come closer together and that at the end of the conference there could be no doubt that pension coverage broadly of the kind proposed in the bill before this house will be made available in all Canada. It is quite true, of course, and indeed it was indicated before the Quebec conference, that the province of Quebec has announced its determination, its decision, to go ahead with a pension plan of its own. It will therefore be necessary for any national plan to work with the provincial plan.
I think it is also obvious that if other provinces, especially other big provinces, decide to go ahead with their own pension plan-and no decision of that kind was indicated at the conference in Quebec-this would make for certain administrative difficulties in regard to the Canada pension plan but would not make a Canada pension plan impossible in any way, shape or form. It is our
view, and I think our view will be shared by many people, that a single national plan is preferable to national coverage by federal and provincial plans. Nevertheless, what I might call the mixed system would be unavoidable if a province or provinces decided to go ahead with their own plan. It is not the intention of the government, Mr. Speaker, to do anything by withdrawing the Canada pension plan to interfere with national coverage and we shall proceed to go ahead with our own plan as put before the house.
During the conference at Quebec the premier of that province gave a very useful clarification of his own government's thinking on pensions, and while it would be a breach of confidence for me to discuss his statement in detail, which has not yet been put before his own legislature, I think it is right to say that all those who were at the conference were impressed by what they heard of the Quebec plan. It is not identical, as is known, with the proposed federal plan. I think in some respects it is a less desirable plan than the federal plan, although that might not be true in the minds of those who drew it up for provincial purposes. But it is a plan, and I think this is the important thing, Mr. Speaker, with which it will be possible for a national plan to co-operate, and ensure by that co-operation complete portability between the provincial plan and the national plan. Mr. Lesage, the premier of Quebec, made it quite clear at the conference that he would work with the federal government to ensure that that kind of co-operation takes place if and when both plans are in effect.
No other province, as I have said, indicated at the conference an intention to establish a pension plan of its own. If one or more should do so the federal plan, of course, is so designed that it would still work with other provinces as long as all the provincial plans were compatible with portability, as is the proposed plan for Quebec. This is not, I repeat, to say that in our view a series of provincial plans is the best way to approach this important problem because that would make for administrative difficulty, but the purpose of our initiative in the federal government would be achieved if there was basic pension coverage of a portable nature available to all Canadians. The conference at Quebec city last week made this conclusion plain, that it is the desire of the provincial

Quebec Dominion-Provincial Conference governments and the federal government to achieve this objective in terms that reconcile federal and provincial jurisdictions.
There were other matters that were discussed, some of them of importance and, indeed, in one or two cases of a controversial character. These controversies arose during the discussions. May I refer to the proposal for the extension of family allowances to age 18 that was put on the agenda by the federal government because certain proposals had been made in this house for that purpose. It is our view that the government's proposal for this extension is a simple extension of the program which this parliament legislated in 1944.
No new principle is involved and, in the government's opinion, no constitutional issue is raised by this proposal. The purpose of family allowances is, and always has been, to assist families in the support of children while they are dependant. In 1944, this purpose was pretty well served by establishing 16 as the cut-off age. Most children at that time began to have earnings and comparatively few extended their education beyond that age. The situation has now changed and more and more children remain dependant beyond the age of 16. We propose, Mr. Speaker, continuing the allowance to 18 instead of 16.
In making that extension, we will apply the same tests as to whether a child is dependant as there have been before, and we made that clear to the conference. There was discussion of this subject at the conference and there have been discussions outside the conference, which seem to assume that the present allowances are paid unconditionally to any child up to the age of 16. This is not the case. In order for a family to be entitled to the allowance under the present act, a child must be either at school or unfit to attend school and, in the case of a girl, she must remain unmarried. I should like to make this clear by reading section 4(2) of the Family Allowances Act, 1944:
The allowance shall cease to be payable with the payment for the month when the child: (a) ceases to be maintained by a parent; (b) ceases to be resident in Canada; (c) attains the age of 16 years; (d) dies; or (e) in the case of a female child, marries.
This is the section in the present act. The new proposal, as we attempted to make clear at Quebec, simply maintains the present conditions in the section, but instead of reading "sixteenth birthday", if all proposals were adopted in their present form it would be "eighteenth birthday". This would be the only change made. No jurisdictional question would be applicable, then, to the amendment we propose to the legislation which the parliament of Canada passed in 1944.


Having made clear our view of the constitutional position, I hope, I should like to go on to recognize, as we recognized at the conference, that in the case of Quebec there is a real, practical problem in this area which does not arise in the case of any other province, because in Quebec students of the ages of 16 and 17 already receive from the provincial government an allowance which, although different from the family allowance in form, does have much the same effect. It is the government's intention, therefore, to consider, in the light of the discussions at the federal-provincial conference what we can do to avoid duplication between federal and provincial actions in this field in these age groups.
Now, another subject which received a good deal of discussion at the conference was the proposal of the federal government in respect of loans to students. In examining this question, Mr. Speaker, we discussed some jurisdictional problems which would arise out of a proposal of this kind. Here, again, a constitutional point has been raised, and in some quarters has been emphasized. So far as I know, no one has challenged the right of the federal government to make loans or, as would be the case in this proposal, to guarantee loans through the banks.
The Quebec view, as expressed at the conference, recognized that this is in itself constitutional but added the rider, and I quote from the statement:
-provided they are normal loans on which interest is charged.
The lending may be unconstitutional, it is suggested, because we propose the students should get the loans without paying interest while they are studying. That view on unconstitutionality we are unable to accept. If we have jurisdiction over banking and credit -and that is not challenged-then it seems to me clear that this includes the right to make certain loans especially attractive, if parliament regards that as a policy in the general interest of Canadians.
But here again, hi the implementing of policy, there are certain practical problems, as we recognized when we put this and the previous matter I have mentioned on the agenda for the Quebec conference before bringing a detailed measure before parliament. In many provinces, not only in one province but in many provinces, there are already student loan schemes of various kinds, and so we want to ensure that there are adequate funds for the needs of all students and that they can be borne, where necessary, without burdening the student with interest while he is a student, and yet this can be in an administrative way which will be satisfactory to the provinces. The Quebec

conference provided a good practical discussion of the ways of achieving this objective and, as the communique points out, in our further consideration of the matter we shall take the views of the provinces, as expressed in Quebec, into consideration.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the one subject which provided the most discussion at the conference was that of shared programs and the possibility of provincial governments contracting out for their provinces from certain of these programs. The policy of the federal government in this field, which had been announced more than once before this conference, was stated again at the conference, as I think will be made clear in the opening statement I gave at the conference, and which is now attached to Hansard of last Friday. It is that the federal government is willing to negotiate appropriate contracting out arrangements with any province so desiring, in respect of shared cost programs which are of a continuing or permanent nature and which involve fairly irregular annual expenditures.
Any arrangements worked out, and this was accepted in Quebec last week, should provide (1) that the contracting out should be accompanied by equivalent fiscal and financial compensation; (2) that any contracting out should not prejudice the position of the other provinces which remain in the programs and, (3) that the federal government should do what it could to ensure national standards of services in respect of the shared cost programs. This can be done in a variety of ways by conditional grants, conditional fiscal compensation, and indeed in other non-fiscal ways.
At Quebec, having discussed this question of principle, we made an examination of the major shared cost programs which were appropriate for the application of these contracting out principles. The only province at the conference which indicated its desire to contract out from any of these programs was the province of Quebec, although others thought that there should be more consideration given to provincial wishes, provincial needs and provincial priorities in initiating any new programs, so that the provinces should have more responsibility for the administration of such programs. There is no difference of opinion between the provincial governments and the federal government on that score, and perhaps in the future improvements can be made in that direction if new programs are initiated.
We agreed at Quebec that detailed negotiations should begin at once with any province desiring to contract out of any program, detailed negotiations for each individual program concerning which a province might wish 20220-114
Quebec Dominion-Provincial Conference to contract out by the application of an appropriate formula.
The first phase of contracting out arrangements-and this was put to the conference- would apply to an interim period during which any province would continue the shared program exactly as it is but would receive equal compensation in the form of tax room and equalization payments. Negotiation on these points will be conducted individually with the provinces which so wish and the other provinces would be kept informed, on the understanding, which they have a right to insist on, that contracting out by any province will not affect the programs for the other provinces. New arrangements for contracting out beyond this interim period will also be considered in technical negotiations but they will necessarily raise further issues of policy of concern to all the provinces whatever their future intentions regarding these programs, and so these arrangements which are worked out and informally adopted concerning them would be taken back for general federal-provincial discussion.
I think it is fair to say we came to a very satisfactory agreement at the conference with respect to this question of shared cost programs-how to deal with any province which might wish to contract out from a particular program or from particular programs in such a way as not to prejudice the interest of the others and in such a way as not to prevent the federal government discharging its obligation or doing what it can to ensure comparability of services across the country.
Then we discussed at some length, also, the question of fiscal relations. I may say that discussion on this important subject was very much to the point and very frank, and did indicate as hon. members know, certain differences of opinion not only between the provincial governments and the federal government, as one would expect-such differences have existed at every federal-provincial conference-but also differences of opinion and emphasis in some respects between provincial governments themselves. But there was general agreement that the problem was one of recognizing the needs and responsibilities of both levels of government, federal and provincial, and providing for as fair a division as possible of revenue sources between them in order to meet increasing responsibility.
The provinces made it clear that their responsibilities have increased, were increasing and were not likely to diminish, especially in the fields of education and communication, and that their existing sources of revenue were not sufficient to deal with these increased responsibilities. The spokesmen for the federal government, while recognizing this, emphasized that the federal government had its
1796	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Quebec Dominion-Provincial Conference
own increasing responsibilities to discharge to the Canadian people as a whole-responsibilities to deal with employment and unemployment, to direct economic and fiscal policies in the best interest of the whole nation, to equalize services and ensure comparable development in so far as government can do this, across the whole country; otherwise Canada will become a land of permanent "haves" and "have-nots" and the strains on our unity, already so great, would become intolerable. This was a federal responsibility we could not lose sight of as we discussed ways and means of helping provincial governments to discharge their responsibilities. No federal government can discharge its responsibilities to Canada by weakening itself financially, economically and politically, no matter how great its concern for provincial difficulties and its desire to help the provinces overcome them. I think, Mr. Speaker, we made that position clear to the conference. Therefore, in my view the federal government must remain strong enough financially and constitutionally to do the work allocated to it in our constitution. The spokesmen of the federal government made it known at Quebec that it intends to do what is possible to ensure this, while willing to examine every possible way of helping the provinces. As the communique states, there must be "mutual accommodation to reconcile their expenditure and revenue requirements."
For the current fiscal year, Mr. Speaker, that accommodation has been made, and it has been made I think in terms which do indicate the desire of the federal government to assist the provinces whenever that is possible. The accommodation made last November did not meet with the wishes of all the provinces, and no financial accommodation I have ever read about in these relations between the federal government and the provinces has at any time met the wishes of all the provinces. But it was laid down at our conference last November that certain changes could take place, and they have been reflected in our budget which has resulted in an additional amount of expenditure being transferred by the federal government to the provinces of $87,448,000. The arrangements for the current year had been made then, in November, so that in this matter the conference last week at Quebec was looking ahead beyond the current year. It was looking ahead in terms of the immediate necessities of the provinces, and we recognize those immediate necessities as we recognize our own. But we have been looking further ahead from the immediate necessities, and we agreed right away that to look ahead was to try to get away if we could from the ad hoc, piecemeal approach to this problem which has been followed over the years.

It was in that spirit that I proposed at the conference an approach toward finding a solution for these fiscal problems, an approach which I believe had never been made before.
I suggested that the federal-provincial conference as a body-not the federal government, not a provincial government, but the federal-provincial conference as a body- should institute immediately a joint examination and review of this whole problem of fiscal relations. It would be a review of the nature and extent of federal-provincial taxes in addition to the financial responsibilities which nowadays have to be carried both by provincial and federal governments. It would be a review, as we put it in the communique, in depth, but it would be undertaken with all possible speed with the aim of producing a definite report by an early date in 1965. This proposal, which is in the communique, was welcomed by the premiers of all the provinces; indeed it was warmly endorsed by them. We in the federal government are now working on detailed proposals for the composition and terms of reference of a tax structure committee which we will be submitting to the provinces without delay. We will then ask the provinces, following the general agreement as to the desirability of the inquiry in itself, whether they will agree to take part by nominating a representative to the committee.
Perhaps I could conclude by reading what I said on this point at the last meeting of the conference:
I think that our discussions have shown one thing above all with unquestionable clarity: we have not been getting to the roots of our problems. Our uncertainties take varying shapes, but we have in common a real uncertainty as to the nature of contemporary federal-provincial relationships within confederation.
We all know that the answer to this problem will determine our survival, will govern our future as a federal state extending from coast to coast. We all know also that we will not find an answer through the kind of piecemeal consideration we have been giving to it. At our recent meetings we have been, I think, fairly successful in finding ad hoc solutions to points of immediate difficulty. As a group we have been reasonably adept at partial solutions and finding political and financial expedients. That Is useful and essential. But it is not enough. We have to go deeper. The question is how.
Then I said:
My suggestion is this: We as a conference should appoint a committee consisting of one minister from each provincial government and, say, two or three from the government of Canada. We should charge that committee, which would have to have full-time experts, to review the nature and extent of federal and provincial taxes in relation to the financial responsibilities which now have to be carried by both federal and provincial governments.
This would be no ordinary committee. The inquiry will require great wisdom and expert knowledge. It will also require devotion to the ideal

of a strong federal government and strong provincial governments, working together for the realization of a prosperous and united confederation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a speech which began almost apologetically ended on a note of promise for the future. The setting up of a committee of 13 to look into the whole question of fiscal relations is indeed an indifferent conclusion to a most unsuccessful conference. I am surprised at the need for such committee to be set up because I seem to recollect that the premier of Quebec and the leader of the Liberal party, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), met together just one year ago and publicly agreed that the Liberal party had the solution to these problems. Now one year later we have the admission on the part of the Prime Minister that all they have had to date have been piecemeal, haphazard, ad hoc decisions; but now a new vista has opened before him and those associated with him which will bring about a new fiscal arrangement. As far as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) is concerned, he said on his arrival in Quebec; "I bring you no blank cheque". I am sure that all the premiers when they left agreed that that is exactly what they got following three days of discussion-a cheque completely blank, not filled out in any particular.
I do not want to go beyond the scope of the discussion which can take place at this point, but I am sure, Mr. Speaker, you would not consider it improper or out of place if I were to suggest that the Liberal party when in opposition had plans for Canadian unity to solve these problems, and to solve them finally and definitely. Now less than a year later we find divisions, cleavages and fissures in the Canadian confederation never equalled throughout the years since 1867. We believe -and there is no division between us and the government in this connection-that the strength of confederation is the major responsibility and objective if the federal system is to be maintained in law as well as in spirit. The Prime Minister has endeavoured to leave the impression that the recent conference was successful. It was a success in that it brought these various representatives together and they left in such good spirits; but the almost unanimous view of Canadians as a whole is that it was an abject failure. Indeed, to realize this one has only to read the press statement that was issued by Premier Lesage, which incidentally has not been filed or added as an appendix to Hansard, which set forth his view of that conference. No matter how much diplomatic finesse is apparent in the final communique, the conference was one of complete innocuity.

Quebec Dominion-Provincial Conference
I am not going to refer in particular to the various matters with which the Prime Minister has dealt. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister smiles. I saw a picture of him in the Toronto Star and it said, "Pale Prime Minister speaks to press". This is the first time in history, sir, that I have known that difficulties changed the colour of one's hair from grey to black. The picture is well worth studying because it indicates that the day of marvels is not yet passed. We have heard about the doctrines of co-operative federalism. Do you remember, sir, what we used to hear about this? Co-operative federalism has in 12 months become synonymous with the epigram "60 days of decision".
What about the opening statement? The Prime Minister went before that conference and his remarks were limited to generalities. His only definiteness throughout the entire statement was with respect to contracting out provisions. The proposals advanced, as outlined in that speech, were indefinite, vague and general; there was nothing indicated of the leadership which we were led to believe would be given at this conference. In essence the proposals added up to vague declarations of good will and hopes of the future as to what might take place in the years ahead. I said there was no plan. There was, however, one striking plan placed before the premiers. It was that if the provinces would take over the administration of the act in regard to hospitalization, the Prime Minister would turn over to the provinces up to 40 per cent of the income tax. Well, sir, that plan had about the same hope of acceptance as if he had said they would turn over all the income tax to the provinces provided they took over the national debt of Canada.
That is the uncertainty here. This was a make-believe conference; one in which no action was taken, no determination was made; and it concluded with the expression of the desire of setting up a committee of 13, which has all the appearances of window dressing designed to conceal the failure of the federal government to have any plans to place before the conference.
I am very much concerned with the extension of contracting out. Is this one Canada, or is it not? Is it appropriate that the federal government should endeavour, or almost express the desire to engage in contracting out? Is it not a fact, sir, that contracting out, carried on to the degree envisaged by the Prime Minister, will mean in time the legalization of the de-confederation of our nation; the piecemeal dismemberment of the basic principles of confederation? Surely the Liberal party today does not subscribe to the disintegration of our country through setting up a variety of plans in every part of our country
1798	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Quebec Dominion-Provincial Conference covering such matters as come within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada? And yet that is where the diplomatic dawdling of one year on the part of this government has brought this nation. It has been diplomatic. The Prime Minister was diplomatic when the premier of Quebec set forth what he wanted in the month of April, 1963; and today the same situation prevails. But what does the premier of Quebec now say? As far as the Canada pension plan is concerned, which is still referred to as a national plan, I am not going into details at this time before we have the opportunity to debate that matter; but does anyone say a national plan can be envisaged with one, or two, or more provinces abstaining? What has taken place in the thinking of the government? Only a month or so ago the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) said-and this was also said during the Ontario election- that if more than one province refused to go into the plan, that would be the end of it. What has taken place in the interval to change that thinking? The Prime Minister says they would establish what he called a mixed system. I agree that never in the history of this country has a government been more qualified for that description in its dealings with the affairs of this nation.
Then there is the question of family allowances. There was no question, according to the Prime Minister, that they were entirely within the jurisdiction of the federal government, without regard to the fact that a rider is attached providing that the children eligible for this payment continue in school. What does the premier of Quebec say following this wonderful meeting of minds, to use the expression that was indulged in on one or two occasions by one of the officials close to the throne? What happened in this meeting of minds? The premier of Quebec says he is going to challenge this in the courts. A year ago there was happiness in the family as between the federal Liberals and the provincial Liberals; they saw eye to eye. Now they see eye into eye. They look at one another with that challenge, and they are going into the courts. That is what this country has been brought to within a few short months.
Then there is the question of loans to students. This is the substitute sop for the plan that was promised to the student body of Canada-10,000 scholarships. What has happened to the scholarships? They have gone with the Canada development corporation.

speechtext:
One wonders how a
government could have found itself in such difficulty in so short a time. There was reference to the setting up of this committee. We have had any number of discussions with regard to looking into the problems of taxation and the fiscal relations between the federal government and the provinces. We have had a royal commission on that subject and now, after all these divisions and separations, the only part of the remarks of the Prime Minister that showed any enthusiasm was as he placed before us that nebulous scheme that holds out, as Mr. Lesage has said, no hope for the problem that is faced by this nation at this time.
I am not going to quote from the various press references on this occasion, but I do say that the premiers of Canada generally went home not only unsatisfied but uncertain as to the future of this country. I do not want to read into the record the press statement made by the premier of Quebec, so I will only refer to one or two comments. In so far as the plan for the committee of 13 is concerned he said:
-it was agreed that action would quickly be taken to study the mechanism of contracting out and of applying them.
He said they would look into that. On the second subject and an equally fundamental one, that of fiscal arrangements, with regard to which a committee of ministers will make a study in depth, he had this to say:
If we have understood the correct interpretation of the project, this would be the true and deep justification for the intergovernmental committee which has been proposed-I merely said that we would like to give further thought to this question before making a statement.
The Prime Minister said today it has been agreed to, so it must have been agreed to since this press statement was made by the premier of Quebec. But then the premier of Quebec went on to say:
For this committee in itself does not settle, nor does it promise to settle with the dispatch which we believe indispensable, the problem of fiscal arrangements-
Then he quotes words he used in the brief and goes on to say:
These words and the tone of urgency in which they were couched were not written without sober thought. Very precisely they mean that we do not believe that Quebec can wait any longer for steps to be taken.
Here we have a renewal of the ultimatums of last April that were delivered by the ministers of that government. Nothing is said about an increase in the share of the provinces in the taxation field, but the premier of Quebec had this to say:
-three figures, 25-25-100, cannot remain a dead issue__We must say that the government of Quebec is not satisfied-

Then he goes on to say with regard to education that what has been done in the two most recent initiatives of the federal government constitute encroachments on the most important sector of provincial jurisdiction, that of education. He says that loans to students are in the same position. Then he goes on to say:
-we cannot accept that the federal administration commit the error, regardless of the good faith in which it would be committed, of thus invading a field which is incontestably of our jurisdiction and which, furthermore, we have occupied for the past three years.
Yet in the face of that the Prime Minister tries to leave the impression that all is well. Sir, a great challenge has come to this country, a challenge whether or not we are going to have one Canada, which has been the policy of the Conservative party from the days of Macdonald and Cartier to today. What happened at this conference constitutes a challenge to that whole concept; and it is not the provinces that are responsible for what has taken place, for the tremendous upheaval in the thinking of the people of Canada. Those responsible sit in the government ranks on the treasury benches. A year ago they said they had the answers; today they say that a committee of 13 may have the answers.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING IN QUEBEC CITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's report on the federal-provincial conference held in Quebec city last week was interesting but discouraging. Many had hoped that at this conference the heads of the governments of Canada would be able to demonstrate a measure of statesmanship that would prove they were conscious of the fact that the greatness of a country depends on more than just the sum total of its parts. One became conscious as the conference proceeded that the representatives of some parts of Canada seem to have lost sight of the fact that they were Canadians as well as speaking for the provinces which they represented.
The Liberal party has always boasted that it and it alone can provide national unity in Canada. I want to say that if last week was a demonstration of the Liberal party's idea of national unity, then heaven help us in the years that lie immediately ahead.
The Prime Minister has mentioned three matters and X should like to say a word or two about each of them. The first is the Canada pension plan. We welcome the statement of the Prime Minister that it is the intention of the government to proceed with this plan even though some of the provinces may institute plans of their own. So far the only province that has indicated definitely that it will proceed with a provincial plan is the province of Quebec. I do hope that
6. 1964	1799
Quebec Dominion-Provincial Conference every effort will be put forth to persuade the province of Ontario to join the federal plan.
There is one feature which I am sure is of interest to the premier of Ontario and which in my opinion is negotiable. That is the matter of the funds under the plan which are available for investment. In its original form there was no division of the funds with the provinces. In the measure now before the house I believe the proposal is that 50 per cent of the funds will be available for provincial investment. It may be that the provinces, particularly the province of Ontario, would settle for a larger percentage of that fund, and I personally can see no objection to agreeing to 75 per cent or 80 per cent of the fund being used for provincial investment. If that would keep Ontario in the plan I think it ought to be proposed to them.
There is one thing I hope the government will not do. I hope it will not agree to any further curtailment of the benefits which are to be made available to the contributors and participants in the plan. The Prime Minister said, if I took down his words correctly, that "pension coverage will be made available in all of Canada." I assume he means by this that every person in Canada will be covered by a provincial plan or the federal plan. This will at least be better than nothing. But a patchwork plan, with some people belonging to a provincial plan and some to a federal plan and where no matter how many administrative difficulties are resolved there will still be an abundance of red tape as people move from one part of the country to the other, will be a plan that is second best to the original idea of a Canada-wide pension plan.
I hope too that if the government is not able to persuade the provinces of Quebec and Ontario to forgo the establishment of provincial plans it will revert to the plan which it envisaged last July, which was much more generous to the participants and which was trimmed down deliberately by the government in order to meet the objections of certain provincial premiers.
The second thing to which the Prime Minister made reference was loans to students and the extension of family allowances to cover those 16 and 17 years of age who are still attending school. I hope the government will proceed with both of these measures, irrespective of any threats to test their constitutionality in the courts. I am not a constitutional expert, but I am sure the government has looked into this matter. The federal government already guarantees bank loans for home improvements, for small businessmen, for fishermen, for farmers and for
1800	HOUSE OF
Quebec Dominion-Provincial Conference municipalities. Certainly the guaranteeing of loans to students, even though part of the interest is to be forgiven, would seem unlikely to raise any serious constitutional problem.
So far as family allowances are concerned, these have been unchallenged for years, and the extension of the age from 16 to 18 ought not to seriously affect and will not, in my opinion, seriously affect the principle.
The third thing to which the Prime Minister has made reference is the shared programs. I want to say to the Prime Minister that I was disappointed that he, in his opening statement, raised this whole question of shared programs, and raised it in a way which in my opinion will do great harm to the bonds that hold confederation together. I readily admit there are many shared programs that need to be reexamined. There are many conditional grants which are much too rigid, with the result that the provinces cannot make effective use of them. A number of the shared programs should be reexamined and in some cases discarded in return for some form of unconditional grant, some further tax abatement or a further adjustment in the equalization grants.
The Prime Minister himself, in his opening statement, selected the hospital insurance plan to illustrate that it might be possible to turn this program over to the provinces in return for a 13 per cent abatement in personal income tax. I know that this agreement has not been concluded, but the Prime Minister's statement amounted to an offer. I hope that the house and the government will keep in mind what is involved if the Prime Minister's offer is accepted. Health and welfare programs are part of the atmosphere that produces a sense of identity in a country. The fact they are Canadians entitles them- from one part of this country to the other, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, to enjoy certain basic health and welfare rights, not because they come from Prince Edward Island or British Columbia but because they are Canadian and have inalienable rights, is the thing that gives people a Canadian identity. The fact they are Canadians entitles them- without any red tape or having to fill out provincial forms or go through a lot of administrative bureaucracy-to these benefits wherever they are in Canada and, in certain cases, wherever they are in the world.
Now, we are destroying this concept the moment we turn hospital insurance over to the provinces. It is all right to say that for the first few years one of the conditions of receiving tax abatement will be adherence to certain national standards. How is the federal government going to enforce such standards? With the passage of time these


plans will change in each province. They have changed already in some provinces. Some provinces charge so much a day, some have a sales tax and some have a per capita tax. There are already variations. I submit that in a quarter of a century we will not recognize the hospital insurance plan if the day comes when its administration and financing is done by ten separate governments.
There is a more serious objection. The Liberal party has been committed for 40 years to the establishment in Canada of a comprehensive national health insurance program, jointly operated by the federal and provincial governments. The logical development was to extend the hospital insurance plan and add to it step by step the various health programs such as medicare, dental care and optomertic care, drugs and other health services. The day that hospital insurance is fragmented between the provinces across Canada, the hope of extending that program into a comprehensive national health insurance program goes down the drain. I hope the government will think this matter over very carefully before proceeding along the lines outlined by the Prime Minister.
I recognize that there is a problem in the province of Quebec and that the government may have to make special arrangements for that province. I ask the government, in making special arrangements for the province of Quebec, not to forget one very basic principle, namely that a concession made to Quebec which might help Quebec will not help the other provinces, and that the government has to keep in mind the differential in the per capita revenue from taxes levied in the different provinces. The giving of a tax abatement to the province of Prince Edward Island will never allow Prince Edward Island to operate a hospital insurance plan or a comprehensive health program. The small provinces must not be lost sight of in the government's desire to appease the very legitimate aspirations of the two larger provinces. These smaller provinces cannot manage these health and welfare programs alone, even if the government gives them a tax abatement. They have not the revenue resources at their disposal to manage programs which, if the government thinks they are expensive today, will be tremendously more expensive within the next decade or two.
I say to the government that while special concessions and special arrangements may have to be made with the province of Quebec because this is a bilingual and bicultural country, I hope the government will not adopt policies that will fragment the rest of Canada.
I am saying to the government that the statement outlined by the Prime Minister of

Canada the other day in Quebec city is a serious one. If the government proceeds with it they are setting their feet along a trail that will lead to the weakening and balkanization of Canada and with it the loss of a sense of identity without which no people can become a great nation.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING IN QUEBEC CITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this not being the time to debate the matter my remarks will be brief. I am convinced, however, that we are dealing with what is the most serious and most critical single problem we have in Canada.
As I listened to the remarks of the previous speakers I could not help but think that perhaps in this situation we have an important role to play as a house of minorities. This is something which does not concern one party but which concerns all of us as representatives of the Canadian people. This is no time for a partisan approach to this problem. We must somehow join hands, both provincially and politically, to try to find an answer to the problem before Canada ceases to be a nation at all.
Speaking very briefly to the several points which have been mentioned, so far as pensions are concerned there are two basic objectives behind any pension plan, be it provincial or federal. These are that security be guaranteed to our people, particularly when because of age or for other reasons they are no longer able to earn their own living; and second that the arrangements which provide this security be made on such a basis that portability will permit an individual to carry that security which he must have, and which we all desire him to have, with him, regardless of the conditions or situation in which he finds himself.
I am concerned whether or not we can have a truly national plan if 30 per cent or 65 per cent of our people, because of the actions of their governments in their particular provinces, refuse to go along with it. I would caution the government not to proceed too quickly just because it was its original intention to bring about a national pension plan, for fear that it may bring in a program that will defeat the very purpose which it is intended to accomplish.
Whether it be a unanimously agreed plan or whether some of the provinces choose to opt out, the fact remains that it must be a pension plan which will have some degree of uniformity if it is to guarantee the portability and security which we are attempting to achieve. Therefore I trust the government will not plunge into this thing because of any commitments it may have made previously, and I urge it to proceed cautiously, having regard not only to the provincial aspects but to the economic situation in Canada.
Quebec Dominion-Provincial Conference
In relation to family allowance extension and student loans, if we have been able to carry on with this phase of our programs without being challenged, as we have in the past, there can be no valid reason for challenging it at this point. These two very important matters, although they may seem minor, must be carried through, and 1 trust they will, because they involve the education of our young people and the provision they must make at this time for their future means of livelihood.
In relation to fiscal policies, and this also includes the shared programs, the federal government should take the lead in setting out a pattern in which the autonomy of the provinces is truly respected. I cannot see how this or any government can continue to hang on to certain responsibilities relating to fiscal policies and shared programs that were taken away from the provinces on a temporary basis during wartime, and which have not been returned since.
I believe all the provinces-remembering there are some that must receive help and others that do not need help, and that because of this somehow there must be a continuing program of equalization-would be much happier if they knew exactly just how far the federal government was going to go in respecting autonomy, and if at the same time the federal government made clear to the provinces the responsibilities they have to maintain in order to secure the necessary funds for our nation to continue as a nation.
This problem will not be solved by dividing ourselves into ten pieces, or by neglecting or paying mere lip service to the basic autonomy we regard as essential for the provinces. In this regard we must remember that Canada is a nation and we all have responsibilities, both individually and as provinces, to this nation. We must remember that there is only one taxpayer in Canada and that all taxes collected by whatever form of government come out of his pocket. That taxpayer is and includes all of us.
Whether we call the answer to the problem co-operative federalism, or whether we call it confederation as it was originally spoken of when we came together as a group of provinces, the fact remains that there must be a foundation on which a nation can stand. Unless we recognize that and give it definite form, then it is impossible to continue as a country.
That is why we must regard this particular statement which the Prime Minister has given as of such magnitude that it is the most important thing we have facing us in this session. Therefore I urge that we all face it from this aspect, and I would ask the government that it take the lead in setting

Quebec Dominion-Provincial Conference up not just occasional federal-provincial conferences-though we have had many in recent months-and not just a study in regard to fiscal policies, but some kind of permanent machinery to make a more careful study of the whole question of confederation to determine by what means we can continue as a nation in Canada.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING IN QUEBEC CITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) may speak about the constitutionality of certain steps taken during the last federal-provincial conference; the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) may continue to play politics with these matters; the leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Douglas) may fear a balkanization of Canada, but there is one thing which still remains and should not be forgotten: we are now experiencing in Quebec a desire, a pride and even more, a passion and an aggressive eagerness to take in our own hands our possibilities, our facilities and our means of development and self-attainment.
That is, Mr. Speaker, the basis of all discussions such as those which were held during the last federal-provincial conference. Exactly a year ago yesterday, the Quebec premier said:
Twelve months will elapse before the next budget is brought down. Either the central government, whichever party comes into office on April 8, will avail itself of the 12 coming months to take into account Quebec's requirements, or we, in Quebec, will have seen to it, during the same period, to make the necessary decisions in fiscal matters.
We have waited a year. That period seemed long to us. During the past year several happenings have stressed the insistence and determination of Quebec to recover and take over control of its destiny and the sovereignty of its means of action.
At that time it claimed 25, 25 and 100 per cent of three sources of income. The majority said: this is only the beginning, we want 100 per cent.
Perhaps some members will not understand what this means, but we know, because we are proud of our destiny and we believe in it.
The federal-provincial conference took place in two stages and ended up as a complete failure, in spite of what the Prime Minister may say, he might shut his eyes on the matter or be blinded by his entourage. It might be that entourage which is mostly to blame, and especially the French Canadian ministers, who far from being brilliant, dared not take their own place and who acted as flatterers and yes-men, rather than being the spokesmen and flag-bearers of the French Canadian people in defence of their deep and fair claims.


The Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) may say that everything is fine, but it is because he is not aware of what is happening at the present time in the province of Quebec. And the other French Canadian ministers can remain deaf and dumb because they care more for their quiet life, their little job, than for the rights of their compatriots within confederation which they should be fighting for.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON MEETING IN QUEBEC CITY
speechtext:
It may be that in the past we, in Quebec, tried again and again to find guilty parties everywhere, without exactly finding the right ones, because in most cases they belonged to our own people.
Many times, in the house, I deemed it advisable to let the present government know how serious and determined the people of Quebec were about their rights. We deemed it advisable to make suggestions, radical sometimes, but always logical, realistic and sensible.
The Prime Minister and his government chose not to listen. The federal-provincial conference is over and we do not hesitate to state that it was a dialogue between deaf people.
We are still talking of the statement made earlier by the Prime Minister on the constitutionality or granting family allowances at 16 or 17 years of age. Since when is there anything in the Quebec legislation making it compulsory to attend school up to 18 years of age? Since when? We believe that is a direct interference of the federal government into the educational field of the province of Quebec. The intrusion first started into well defined fields and as each year goes by we see the federal government intrude in other educational fields. We are determined to put a stop to these intrusions.
Today, following the federal-provincial conference, what do we hear in the province of Quebec? As far as the people are concerned, it has been a failure. The federal-provincial conference was an abject failure, and that fact has been confirmed in editorials published by various newspapers in the province of Quebec.
May I quote only one editorial published in Le Soleil on April 4 and written by Mr. Henri Dutil. It reads as follows:

The last call has really been sounded and we may have seen the last federal-provincial conference. That is the opinion now prevailing in serious circles where the affairs of the nation are discussed daily.
Now, we may read in VAction the following item, signed by Jean Hubert:
The fact that the Quebec premier, Mr. Jean Lesage, considered that he should personally issue a different press release from the official one, points unquestionably to the gravity of the situation.
The problem did not take shape overnight. It is due to growing federal intrusion in provincial affairs, and more particularly in the taxation field.
I shall also quote Mario Cardinal, writing in Le Devoir:
Perhaps confederation never has seemed as publicly threatened and at such a high level.
And there is the large heading of an article by Jean-Pierre Fournier, which says:
Confederation torn apart.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are reports and editorials which deal with the present situation.
We saw students make a public demonstration to try and open the Prime Minister's eyes, during the federal-provincial conference, and make suggestions which were serious in themselves and should have been taken into consideration. But nothing was done. Today, there is some talk about celebrating confederation. Listen to what is being said in the province of Quebec in respect of confederation. Practically nobody there believes in a confederation, the centennial of which should call for a celebration.
And who is responsible? Ottawa has its share of responsibility.
If we take a closer look at that situation, we realize that there are in fact persons to blame, not only in Ottawa, but directly within the provincial government. Incidentally, about that federal-provincial conference, may I point out the stand taken by the Quebec premier on that occasion?
We cannot forget that he was once a member of the federal cabinet which made headway in the spoliation of the rights of French Canadians by the federal government. We cannot forget either that he was then a champion of centralization, here in Ottawa.
We wonder whether it is not for that reason that he is so soft towards infringements by Ottawa.
Now, he claims to be an autonomist, and we are really amazed by the lack of seriousness in his fight against that new centralization.
We only have to recall that when arrangements on taxation rights were made during the last war, to enable the federal government, because of the urgency, to take over certain direct taxes to meet the needs of war, it was provided that after a period of one
Quebec Dominion-Provincial Conference year, an order in council passed by a province could end that centralization of taxation rights. Why does not Mr. Lesage take such a step? Why does he not take back those sources of income and why does he not put an end, in a unilateral manner, to that infringement by the federal government into the field of direct taxation?
Is the premier of the province of Quebec serious when he fights to regain our fiscal rights? Today, we indeed have cause to wonder.
You recall what happened at the time of the last federal-provincial conference. Beaten by Ottawa, he has now changed and wants to turn against the people of Quebec and deprive them through double taxation.
Mr. Speaker, I take advantage of this forum to tell the government of the province of Quebec that when one has rights, he does not discuss, he takes them, especially when the law allows him to do so. I believe it would be appropriate to quote the statement of Premier Manning of Alberta who said, as reported by the newspaper Le Soleil of April 4:
Premier Jean Lesage was not roaring like a lion.
It was laughable to read some accounts of the alleged threats during the federal-provincial conference.
Mr. Speaker, at least we tried discussing, but to no avail.
Studies, committees, conferences, discussions, meetings among 13 ministers, all that, from now on, should end.
From now on, we shall take the necessary democratic means to recover what belongs to Quebec. We shall take those means when and where they are required.
As I said, we have nothing against the other provinces or the other citizens of Canada. We do not want to take anything away from them. We want only what belongs to us and we shall get it.
Mr. Speaker, I shall close my remarks by quoting a sentence of the mayor of Montreal, Mr. Jean Drapeau. As stated in Le Devoir of this morning, Mr. Drapeau said:
There are three different trends among French Canadians: co-operative federalism, a binational confederation and independence for Quebec; there is no doubt that it is mostly between these last two alternatives that some day a choice will have to be made.
Mr. Speaker, I want to repeat this last part of the sentence:
There is no doubt it is mostly between those last two alternatives that some day a choice will have to be made.
And Le Devoir goes on:
Such are the terms, which leave little room for ambiguity, in which the mayor of Montreal,

Mr. Speaker, those words contain no threat and no ultimatum. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to implement the fundamental principle of democracy that the laws of a country should be made only by the elected representatives of the people. Its aim is to remove the possibility of the legislation enacted by the elected representatives being interfered with or delayed by a body of persons which has no mandate from the people of this country. The Senate being such a body this bill proposes its abolition.
Clause 1 of the bill provides that the parliament of Canada shall consist of the Queen and the House of Commons; the rest of the clauses in the bill make the necessary consequential amendments to the British North America Act.
I should like to express my thanks to our parliamentary counsel for his assistance to me in drafting this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Although the detail of the proposed bill is not before the house its stated purpose makes it abundantly clear that no matter how the bill may have been drafted, or by whom, the proposed bill would be unconstitutional. I say this because its effect would be to alter radically in a unilateral manner the composition of the parliament of Canada.
The British North America Act contains guarantees to certain provinces such as Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and more recently Prince Edward Island, whereby the representation in this house from those provinces is linked to the number of senators from those same provinces. To abolish the Senate without the consent of those provinces, and in fact of all the provinces, would be to brush aside constitutional guarantees solemnly made, and as solemnly observed to date, in order to ensure the original entry to and continued participation in Canada of those provinces so affected. The hon. member has not this consent nor could he get it. Further, such a bill would have consequential effects on the Representation Act, the details of which I need not go into but which, I submit, result from the same defect I mentioned previously.
Finally, I submit that it has never been in the contemplation of the constitution of Canada nor in the concept of our parliament that either the House of Commons or the Senate should have the right even to introduce legislation to abolish the other. To concede that the Commons could legislate the abolition of the Senate must lead to the equally absurd proposition that the Senate could legislate the abolition of this chamber. On these limited grounds of unconstitutionality-and there are others-I submit that any proposed bill to abolish the Senate is presently out of order and should not be read even the first time. It is repugnant, sir.

in this house. I am also amazed that my hon. friend, being the learned lawyer he is, referred to these senatorial floors as though they were provided in the original British North America Act. Such is not the case; they were not written into the act until 1915.
Therefore I suggest that the points raised by the hon. member fall to the ground. The fact is that under Section 91A of the British North America Act we have the right to amend our constitution with respect to matters which are exclusively federal. We have already done so with respect to the representation in the House of Commons. There are other bills on the order paper with respect to matters of representation and the qualifications required of a senator. Both the present government and the previous one have made such proposals. I suggest that with regard to the right of this House of Commons to introduce and deal with such a bill and send it on to the other place there is no question whatsoever; and I feel that the advice I received from our parliamentary counsel is superior to the advice which has been tendered to Your Honour by the hon. member for Edmonton West.

speechtext:
The declaration on the elimination of racial discrimination, to which the question refers, was adopted unanimously by the United Nations general assembly last December. While a declaration does not impose any formal obligation on a country which votes for it, it does provide a standard of conduct for members of the United Nations and suggests guide lines for legislation. Most member governments will probably not take at this time any legislative action as a result of the declaration, since the human rights commission, on the instructions of the United Nations general assembly, is engaged in drafting a convention on the elimination of racial discrimination which will be the definitive document. If subscribed to by member states, the convention will require to be implemented and governments will have to consider whether legislation is necessary to carry out the articles of the convention.

Quite apart from these developments at the United Nations, a problem has arisen in Canada resulting from recent outbreaks of racial propaganda. Hon. members will recall the remarks on this subject made by the Minister of Justice to this house on March 10. Later, outside the house, the minister indicated that he favoured the principle of an amendment to forbid racial propaganda and that the real problem is to find a formula which meets the evil upon which all decent men agree without, at the same time, interfering with a proper freedom of speech. He indicated that the matter was being pursued energetically and that appropriate measures would be taken as early as possible when an acceptable formula had been found.
