speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Labour whether Leonard McLaughlin has been placed in control of the S.I.U. administration by the board of trustees?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
speechtext: The answer is no, Mr. Speaker.
What position does he occupy today with the S.I.U.?
My understanding, subject to checking it, is that Mr. McLaughlin is executive vice president of the seafarers' international union.
And has there been no appointment made of Mr. McLaughlin at all, as reported in the press?

No, Mr. Speaker, there has been no appointment of Mr. McLaughlin, 

according to my information from the trustees. Maybe my right hon. friend would permit me to make an observation or two with respect to the agreement or understanding reached between the trustees on the one hand and the president of the seafarers' international union of North America, Mr. Hall, on Friday last.
A public statement was issued enumerating seven points on which an understanding had been reached, one of which, to summarize it, was that immediately steps would be taken to restore the S.I.U. of Canada to the constitutional control of its members. Constitutional provision for succession to the presidency of the seafarers' international union of Canada will be implemented as a first step in restoring their control.
As I understand the situation-and this may assist the Leader of the Opposition-there will be no immediate change in the present leadership of the S.I.U. of Canada until the shipping season is further advanced. This period of time will provide an opportunity to ensure that the arrangements have been fully honoured before any change is made. When the change takes place, Mr. McLaughlin will not be appointed as president by the trustees but, rather, they will allow the provision of the constitution with respect to the succession of leadership to be put into effect. Mr. Turner, I understand, will remain as representative of the trustees who will continue to supervise the over-all administration of the union.
I might conclude by saying that the arrangement as outlined in the joint statement on Friday contemplates a cessation of harassment of all shipping in United States ports, and surely if that does come about, combined with the continued supervision by the trustees-over the S.I.U., a major step forward will have been taken in resolving this problem.
Under the arrangements made between Mr. Hall and the trustees, is it not a fact that in accordance with the succession, McLaughlin will be placed in the position previously occupied by Banks?

I am sorry, but I did not
follow the question put by the Leader of the Opposition. If he would repeat it I would be glad to answer it.

The question is simply this: Was there any arrangement made between Hall and the trustees that McLaughlin should, in the ordinary course of events, follow in the succession and hold the position held by Banks at the time he was removed from office?

I should make it clear that the information I am giving to the

house is information received from the trustees regarding a decision taken by them in their role as quasi administrators of this union. The situation as put forward by the Leader of the Opposition is correct, except, as I have stated, that the trustees will not take any action on their own account to appoint Mr. McLaughlin as president, and this change which is contemplated with the removal of Mr. Turner is not to take place until a period of time has elapsed to make it possible to observe whether the arrangements entered into between the trustees and Mr. Hall are fully honoured.

I should like permission to ask one further question. I am just wondering if McLaughlin has gone through some political dry cleaning, because if one reads the Norris report it says at pages 169 and 170 that he is a clever, resourceful and entirely untruthful witness-that he is devious and adept in carrying out the one-man policies of Banks, and that his subservience to and support of Banks in all circumstances was demonstrated from an early age.
Would the minister not think that this is the last person in the world-
You hate to see it settled.
What did the Prime Minister say?
Apparently you do not want it settled.
If we are to get a settlement by securing the help of a hoodlum like that, I wonder whether or not the cost is too high.

In reply to the comment made by the Leader of the Opposition, may I say this: It is a fact that the passage he referred to appears in the report by Mr. Justice Norris. It is also a fact that the three trustees, consisting of Mr. Justice Dryer, also on the bench of the supreme court of British Columbia, Judge Lippe of Quebec and Mr. Charles Millard, a very experienced unionist of unquestioned integrity, have all been in direct charge of this situation for a period of months, now, and they have concluded, in the exercise of the authority granted them by parliament, that this is an arrangement which will assist in the resolution of these difficulties. In this instance my opinion is not at issue because the trustees are exercising independent authority given to them by parliament.

In view of the fact that the trustees were appointed by parliament, or set up under legislation passed by parliament, and parliament is responsible to the people of Canada for
Inquiries of the Ministry their actions, I should like to ask the Minister of Labour if he considers that taking steps which will lead to the appointment of Leonard J. McLaughlin, described by Mr. Justice Norris as "Banks' man Friday" will carry out the intent and desire of parliament, which was to free the shipping industry from the rule of thugs and to destroy the hoodlum empire which had victimized and terrorized the great lakes shipping industry for too long a period of time.
I should like to ask the minister whether he thinks that appointing Mr. McLaughlin to the post contemplated is likely to carry out that intention?
I must, once again, insist that the trustees are not appointing Mr. McLaughlin to the presidency of the S.I.U.
A play on words.

It is quite clear that they are not appointing him now. I will be the last to suggest that the situation is wholly resolved, but I do maintain it is reasonable for the House of Commons and for the people of Canada to give their support to the trustees, each of whom is a rather considerable person, as they excercise their responsibilities from day to day. They have concluded this arrangement which, if successful-and this remains to be seen, of course-will provide for the complete freedom of Canadian shipping in United States ports and will permit the trustees to continue as supervisors, I was about to say "masters" but that is not the right word, in authority over the S.I.U. of Canada, including Mr. McLaughlin, who may-and it is a question of "may"-after the passage of time, become president in accordance with the constitution of the seafarers international union of Canada.

On a question of privilege. The minister has just made a statement which I think ought to be reconciled with the statement which was issued by the trustees and by Mr. Hall. That statement reads as follows:
Immediate steps will be taken to restore the S.I.U. of Canada to the constitutional control of its members. Constitutional provisions for succession to the presidency of the S.I.U. of Canada will be implemented as a first step in restoring membership control.
I submit that the moment the trustees remove Mr. Turner, who is there at the present time, the office automatically goes to the first executive vice president, who is Mr. McLaughlin. That follows from the constitution. Therefore, it seems to me the minister is playing fast and loose with the house when he seeks to give the impression that the announcement made the other day

Canada Elections Act
does not automatically mean the appointment of Mr. McLaughlin when control has been turned back to the membership.
I want to ask the minister a simple question. Does he think that turning control back to the members, and the appointment of the vice president to the presidency is carrying out the purpose parliament had in mind when it passed the legislation setting up the board of trustees?
The first point is that the government has not taken any action whatsoever.
As usual.

It is an action taken by the trustees under authority given them by parliament. That is the first point to be made. The second point is this-it may appear an unimportant point to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam but this is a very important matter to the membership of the seafarers' international union of Canada, that Mr. McLaughlin, if and when he becomes president, will not become president by appointment by the board of trustees, but by the operation of the constitution of the union itself.
Oh, oh.

Order. It being five o'clock p.m., pursuant to section 3 of standing order 15 the house will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely notices of motions.

On a point of privilege, Mr. Speaker, before you call it five o'clock, do I now understand that the house is allowed to debate every private member's bill on the order paper, according to the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), and is my bill ruled out of order incorrectly?

I really do not see any question of privilege there. It may be a complaint but there is no question of privilege under the rules which, by law, if I may put it that way, I must enforce. Therefore, it being five o'clock it is my duty to call on the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. McNulty).

subtopic: VOTING PRIVILEGES FOR PATIENTS IN PUBLIC HOSPITALS
VOTING PRIVILEGES FOR PATIENTS IN PUBLIC HOSPITALS
speechtext:
That the standing committee on privileges and elections be empowered to consider the advisability of amending the Canada Elections Act in order to provide:
(1)	that persons confined to hospitals be allowed to exercise their franchise in federal elections;
(2)	that portable polls be provided for public hospitals;

(3)	that transfers be allowed up to and including election day for persons confined to hospital; and, for such purposes, to recommend such amendments to the said act as may be deemed advisable.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am proposing in this motion that the standing committee on privileges and elections seriously consider the fact that hundreds of thousands of Canadians in public hospitals are now being denied the right to exercise their franchise. It is my hope that the standing committee will make certain recommendations which will remedy this undemocratic situation.
I realize that this problem has been discussed in committee in a general way, along with other proposed amendments to the Canada Elections Act. I know there are those who feel that it would be very difficult to provide voting privileges to patients in public hospitals. However, Mr. Speaker, I do not feel that the acknowledged difficulties should cause us to wash our hands of the responsibility which we as parliamentarians have, the responsibility to assure to every citizen in Canada the right to cast a ballot.
In a democracy such as ours it is generally agreed that the common good is chiefly guaranteed when personal rights and duties are maintained. Our chief concern as elected representatives must be to ensure that these rights are acknowledged, respected, defended and promoted. All citizens of age have the inviolable right to vote, to state their opinions as to who shall or shall' not govern in a democracy. Patients in public hospital are now denied this basic right. Members of the armed services and their dependants have the right to vote in military hospitals.
With respect, Mr. Speaker, I should just like to read section 27(1) of the Canada Elections Act, which is as follows:
(1) Every Canadian forces elector, as defined in paragraph 20, who is undergoing treatment in a service hospital or convalescent institution during the period prescribed in subparagraph (1) of paragraph 25 for the taking of the votes of Canadian forces electors at a general election shall be deemed to be a member of the unit under the command of the officer in charge of such hospital or convalescent institution, and a Canadian forces elector, as defined in paragraph 20A, whose husband is in such hospital or institution may vote at the place where her husband may vote or at the place where he could have voted before he went in such hospital or institution.
The members of the armed forces, as I say, and their dependants are allowed to vote in military hospitals. Their votes can be counted in their home constituency regardless of where the military hospital is located. Residents of homes for the aged and patients in Department of Veterans Affairs hospitals, sana-toriums and many other like institutions, are allowed to vote and have portable polls. Subsection (2) of section 27 of the act reads as follows:

(2) Whenever deemed advisable by the deputy returning officer who is authorized under these regulations to take the votes at a service hospital or convalescent institution, he shall, with the approval of the officer commanding such hospital or institution, go from room to room to take the votes of the bedridden Canadian forces electors.
In respect to other institutions, Mr. Speaker, section 45(14) of the act provides that:
(14) Whenever a polling station has been established in a sanatorium, a home for the aged, a chronic hospital, or similar institution for the care and treatment of tuberculosis or other chronic diseases, the deputy returning officer and the poll clerk shall, while the poll is open on polling day and when deemed necessary by the deputy returning officer, suspend temporarily the voting in such polling station, and shall, with the approval of the person in charge of such institution, carry the ballot box, poll book, ballot papers and other necessary election documents from room to room in such institution to take the votes of bedridden patients-
It is said, Mr. Speaker, that in many institutions portable polls are allowed under the act at the present time. One matter which has been brought to my attention is that in large urban centres people who are hospitalized may come from different constituencies and it would be difficult to record their votes. In this case perhaps we could set up a central distribution area in each province where public hospital votes could be sent and counted at the same time as the military votes, or they could be counted at some other time to be decided upon. It may be that we might have to set up special returning officers in each public hospital, just as we do in many of the institutions I mentioned previously.
I do not feel it is necessary for people to be present in the hospitals when the election writ is issued. I would hope that a transfer slip or affidavit could be issued which could be signed by the person voting in the presence of the returning officer, just as we now allow poll workers in all constituencies transfers up to and including election day. It is quite possible that we may have to set a time limit, perhaps 48 hours or so, so that the administration and recording of these transfers might be better concluded.
I do not intend to speak longer on this motion, but I should just like to ask the co-operation of all hon. members to allow this motion to go to committee. I am sure that no one in this house would want to deny his fellow citizens their democratic right to vote. I am also confident that the standing committee on privileges and elections would be able to examine all facets of this present problem and come up with a workable solution.

subtopic: VOTING PRIVILEGES FOR PATIENTS IN PUBLIC HOSPITALS
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I want to commend the mover of 20220-115
Canada Elections Act
this notice of motion, and I am very pleased to second it. As he has mentioned, people who are confined in such institutions as tuberculosis sanatoria or hospitals for the chronically ill, or who reside in a senior citizen's home, have a vote in a general election. All hon. members realize that at the present moment patients in a general hospital are not able to vote on election day. I should also like to point out to hon. members that if you happen to be in hospital at the time of enumeration, and are an urban voter, unless you are actually out of hospital by the time additions to the voters' list are made, you could be left off the voters' list despite the fact that you might have left the hospital and be quite fit to vote on election day.
At the present time veterans in D.V.A. hospitals have a vote. Veterans in any hospital have a vote, even if they are in an ordinary, public, general hospital, if they are being treated under the auspices of the Department of Veterans Affairs. The only difference is as to where the vote is actually counted. If the patient is in a D.V.A. hospital that has over 25 veterans, the vote is counted at their normal place of residence, no matter what part of Canada that might be. If the patient is being treated under the auspices of the Department of Veterans Affairs in a non-veteran hospital, his vote is actually counted in the poll where the vote is cast; that is, in the poll in which the hospital is situated. As the hon. member has mentioned, a veteran can vote even if he is incapacitated; the voting box can be carried from bed to bed. I should like to point out, also, that it could happen in an ordinary, general, public hospital where the person in question was a veteran and was under treatment by the Department of Veterans Affairs, that he would have a vote and three other people in the same room, because they were non-veterans, would not have a vote. I think this is unfair. I believe that everybody in the room should have the right to vote in a general election.
As an ex-physician 1 should like to state that most people who are in hospital are physically fit to vote. There are very few people in hospital who are so physically ill that they are not able to cast a ballot. Just as an example I should like to point out that almost all the occupants of a maternity ward would be quite capable of getting up and going anywhere in the hospital to cast a ballot. Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about how many people lose the franchise because of their hospitalization. This does not include those who lose their vote because they are in hospital at the time of enumeration. With regard to the average number of patients in hospital in any one day

Canada Elections Act
in Canada, in 1961 this number was 176,000. However, we have to exclude those people in tuberculosis sanatoria or chronic illness hospitals, who do have a vote now; and we have to exclude the mental patients who, even with the changes in the act suggested by the hon. member would still not have a vote. The figures for 1961 shown in the budget review for general hospitals indicate that on any one day there are approximately 73,000 people in these hospitals. As we all realize, all these people would not have a vote; some of them would be children under the age of 21 and some would not normally have a vote because they were non-Canadian. But we are speaking here generally of between 40,000 and 50,000 people being unable to exercise their franchise because they were in hospital.
I feel very strongly about this, and I am sure all hon. members have received many complaints from people in their constituencies during election campaigns to the effect that just because they were in hospital they could not cast their ballot. The notice of motion brought forward by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. McNulty) would correct this situation and I hope hon. members will support this resolution.

subtopic: VOTING PRIVILEGES FOR PATIENTS IN PUBLIC HOSPITALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would certainly like to congratulate the hon. member who has proposed this resolution. I think in a day and age where we have seen, for example, many improvements in our advance polling facilities we realize that in many areas people who normally would have a right to vote should not be deprived of their vote. As I say, we have seen this taking place in recent years, when there have been many improvements in rural and urban areas in relation to advance polling facilities. The hon. member who has so wisely brought this subject before the House of Commons has now raised the matter of voting privileges for those confined to hospital. I think the hon. member who has just spoken has underlined the importance of the word "hospital" being given the broadest possible definition. In order to make this resolution and the study of it really meaningful, I think all hon. members will agree that the widest possible definition must be given to the word "hospital".
I am not quite sure, but I think the hon. member who has just spoken-who has had much experience in this field-made a direct reference to nursing homes. At the same time I should like to raise the subject of people who are actually sick and confined to their own homes. I think this is particularly true of sparsely settled rural areas which do not have the hospital facilities we would like them to have. Many advances have been made

in recent years, but this situation is one of the facts of life. I know a great many old, and young, people who are sick and confined to their homes who are often, I think, unfairly, deprived of the right to vote. I hope this subject will be referred to the committee, as the hon. member has requested, and I hope the broader subject to which I have made reference will be included in the study. I am sure I speak for many hon. members when again I congratulate the hon. member for bringing this most important subject before the House of Commons this afternoon.

subtopic: VOTING PRIVILEGES FOR PATIENTS IN PUBLIC HOSPITALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to speak for very long on this resolution because, like the other hon. members who have spoken, I favour the resolution and think it would be very helpful if the legislation were passed. We are all anxious that everybody entitled to vote should not be prevented by illness or anything beyond their control from having the right to do so. The effect of passing this resolution will no doubt be that the appropriate legislation will be drafted and perhaps referred to the committee on privileges and elections which, when it is reconstituted, will be considering detailed amendments to the Canada Elections Act. I think it is important that we do consider the actual detailed legislation, because while it is perfectly right that everyone confined to hospital should not on that account be deprived of their franchise, it is also important that consideration should be given to the conditions under which they are called upon to vote.
There have been some instances called to my attention-not in my own constituency, I must say-where it would appear that people, older people particularly in certain institutions, are sort of lined up by attendants and others to vote. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Harley) said that many people in hospital were physically fit to vote and were not unable to vote by reason of being physically disabled; but there may sometimes be people in hospital who are mentally quite unfit to vote and yet are induced by kindly persuasion to vote when they have no knowledge at all of what they are doing. I think this aspect of the matter should be considered when the actual legislation bringing this measure into effect is brought forward. I think we should all be brief and to the point in dealing with this particular resolution, Mr. Speaker, because it would be an excellent thing if its intent were put into effect.
Sometimes these private members' hours seem rather futile; nothing is passed and nothing much is done. I suggest it would be a good thing if we would pass this resolution,

which we all approve of in principle, and indicate to those responsible for redrafting the Canada Elections Act that all parties in the house, all members of the house, I think, desire that the arrangements to vote for people who are ill in hospital should be effectively carried out.

subtopic: VOTING PRIVILEGES FOR PATIENTS IN PUBLIC HOSPITALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part very briefly in the debate on the motion before the house. I think we all realize that one of the main objectives of the Canada Elections Act should be to enable the greatest possible number of electors to exercise their franchise. Unfortunately, it almost appears at times as though the effects are just the opposite. In the light of experience and observation I believe that we should seek constantly to improve our election machinery, especially with regard to problems that are beyond the control of the electors, and certainly the motion before us now is in that category.
In many instances the percentage of those who vote is lamentably small. In some nations the law requires electors to vote or face a penalty. However, the motion before us is not designed to prod the careless but rather to assist those who are willing to vote but who, because of circumstances, are unable to make their way to the polling stations. Illness is not a condition that one can regulate. It cannot be decided that illness or surgical operations shall only take place in the period between elections. In fact, in the last few years especially the period between elections has been so short that it would be ridiculous to think of any such situation.
Therefore I believe that in so far as possible our election machinery should be such that those who are stricken with illness will not be deprived of their democratic right to vote. I realize, of course, that there may be some problems and disadvantages such as have been referred to by other speakers today, especially in regard to the conducting of portable polls, but I believe that the dangers inherent in such a procedure can be minimized or completely eliminated once we decide that this is the fair and just thing to do.
One hon. member who spoke referred to the approximate number of people who are deprived of their right to vote under the present circumstances. I do not believe that the number is necessarily the criterion. I believe it is essential that we do our very best to see that every single person who can has the opportunity to exercise his or her franchise by marking the ballot and choosing those who will become their representatives in the legislative bodies of this nation. Therefore we support the motion and we trust that
Canada Elections Act
the house will give favourable consideration to it, to the end that it may be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections for consideration.

subtopic: VOTING PRIVILEGES FOR PATIENTS IN PUBLIC HOSPITALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. McNulty) for bringing to the attention of the house this aspect of voting, which has been neglected in the past. I should like to bring to the attention of members of the house particularly the fate of people in nursing homes. I come from a constituency in which there are at least 17 nursing homes, each of them containing anywhere from 20 to 50 patients. True, not all of these unfortunate people are in a mental state to cast a rational vote under our democratic system. However, there are many people confined to nursing homes who are there because they were unable to get a bed in a general hospital or a convalescent hospital. Therefore, on account of some physical disability, and no mental disability at all, they have been deprived in the past of the right to cast their vote at federal elections.
That is why I should like to give notice that if this motion, as it should, reaches the standing committee on privileges and elections that committee should also consider the importance of granting voting polls in nursing homes in the constituencies across the country. At the same time I should like to associate myself with the views of hon. members who have emphasized the need also of extending the franchise to people who are in general hospitals at the time of a federal election vote.

subtopic: VOTING PRIVILEGES FOR PATIENTS IN PUBLIC HOSPITALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. McNulty) for having introduced this notice of motion. However, having been a member of the committee on privileges and elections last session and also being aware of the fact that this matter was discussed by the same committee in 1960, may I say I do not think any of the speakers today have dealt sufficiently with the practical difficulties involved in extending the franchise to people in hospitals throughout the country. It is all very well to state as a broad principle that we should enfranchise as many people as possible. However, there are practical difficulties with many groups of people, and because of the impossibility of policing the act or preventing abuses of the act or because of the extreme cost involved we are just not able to enfranchise them under the existing act.
When this matter was brought before the committee on privileges and elections last session we reached the conclusion that it was not practically possible to enfranchise people

Canada Elections Act
in hospital without having a permanent voters list and a system of absentee voting. It was on this premise and for other reasons that the committee passed the following motion: That a study be undertaken under the chairmanship of the chief electoral officer for the preparation of a full report on the question of a permanent electors list and of a method of absentee voting, stating the arguments for and against the adoption of a permanent list; and
That the committee recommend to the government that it approach the governments of the provinces with a view to participating in such a study and to canvass the possibility of a joint permanent electors list.
After the bill establishing a commissioner of elections was passed last session, one of the terms of reference he was given was to conduct a study in detail of the question of a permanent voters list. He has the necessary funds and staff to undertake such a study. This matter has been discussed by many committees in the past but they were always a little shy of information on which to form any valid conclusions. I suggest that we are moving in this direction, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps we will have a permanent voters list and an absentee voting system, with the result that many of the difficulties I propose to raise now may not be valid in the future.
However, the chief electoral officer raised the point in committee that under the present act it was not possible or practical to extend the franchise to people in hospitals. Even if we did have these portable polling booths for hospitals, it would be impossible to process the ballots adequately, allot them to their respective electoral districts and still preserve the secrecy of the ballot. Reference was made this afternoon to the fact that we do have voting in veterans hospitals. This, of course, is true but it is done under a special provision of the armed forces voting regulations. Under these regulations it is necessary for the veteran to indicate at the beginning of the year what his electoral district is. This of course is the key to absentee voting, and is the procedure followed in connection with veterans hospitals. We are informed also by the department of health and welfare that the average stay in acute hospitals in this country is ten days.
In view of the provisions in the act now for advance polls, and the fact that most people who are going to find themselves in hospitals on polling day have an opportunity to vote at an advance poll, I do not think we need this change. All of us here who are involved in elections know that we cannot protect an uninformed citizenry against themselves. We have all received calls just before election day asking where a person can vote because he is going to be out of town. We have to inform these people that the advance polls are held on the Saturday

and Monday of the week prior to voting day. These people feel they are being disfranchised. The provisions of the act are clear and the newspapers carry stories about the advance voting days, yet some people do not avail themselves of these provisions. I suggest that many people who find themselves in hospitals are in the same situation. They just have not availed themselves of the provisions which are already in the act for advance polls.
The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) raised the question of chronic institutions and nursing homes. Well, we do have provisions under the act for people in chronic institutions such as nursing homes, sanatoria, old age homes and other chronic hospitals. When the person is a resident of the institution on enumeration day, he is permitted to vote. I believe, however, the hon. member was referring to the smaller nursing homes that do not have a poll on the premises and it is impossible for these people to get out to a poll. This is quite a different matter and one that perhaps the committee should study. We could, perhaps, have portable stations for these institutions. The other difficulty in connection with extending voting to hospitals is that in many of our hospitals there are people who are not normally resident of the electoral district in which the hospital is located. This creates some serious difficulties in attempting to extend the franchise to these people. The hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) suggested in the committee that perhaps 90 per cent of these people were actually residents of the riding in which the hospital was located, and we could make special provisions for them.
I feel, however, if we had a portable polling booth in these hospitals and some people were allowed to vote while others were not, this would be even more demoralizing to the patients. It would again point up the differences between rural voters and urban voters. In a metropolitan centre such as Toronto we might have people in hospitals from 30 or 40 electoral districts, and we would have to have a portable booth and a returning officer for each constituency. It would become extremely difficult. If we adopt some other form, like a ballot with an envelope on which we write in the constituency, it would still be difficult to preserve the secrecy of the ballot because we would have to indicate to whom this ballot belonged. In other words, the ballot would have to be checked against the voters list for the riding. The results would come in late and we would be faced with the same problems as exist in connection with the armed forces vote, when the returns come in a week later. There would only be

a few people involved and the secrecy of the ballot would certainly be violated. I can see many difficulties in carrying out such a proposal.
The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. McNulty) also proposed some sort of method for transferring the ballot under which you get a transfer authorization. Again, the same problems exist. The transfers for which provision is made today are from one polling station to another within the same riding, and therefore the riding list can be checked to identify the elector. When we get to a situation of transferring ballots from one riding to another, the difficulty of getting these ballots back to the proper ridings and getting the vote recorded would be great.

However, they do not have any say about when an election will take place, and many months before the universities close they have succeeded in obtaining jobs elsewhere in order to earn money to pay for their tuition fees. Under the act they have a choice of either voting at their university or in their home constituency, but they end up 200 miles from either point and they are not willing to travel 200 miles at their own expense to vote.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the principle of the motion but I must congratulate the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Moreau) for indicating some of the difficulties involved in implementing the proposal contained in it. As he said, this matter was discussed in the committee on privileges and elections in 1960 and again in 1963. The dilemma in which we find ourselves is that though there may be considerable difficulties in implementing the principle of the motion, nevertheless we are all of one mind in saying that the benefits of implementing it outweigh the difficulties involved.
The one solution that seems to remove the difficulties suggested by the hon. member for York-Scarborough, and the one which would also enable those people referred to by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More) to exercise the franchise, would seem to be a permanent voters list and some kind of absentee voting. I am inclined to feel, at least from the evidence which came forward at the last meeting of the committee on privileges and elections, and from the reference that committee made to the previous committee, that the difficulties are many.
One hon. member suggested, and I do not know whether I agree with his suggestion, that if there were a difference between urban and rural constituencies so far as the residency of a patient is concerned, perhaps the solution would be to make the hospital part of the constituency in which it is located. For instance, in the riding of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador it is reasonable to assume that the vast majority of patients in the principal hospital would be from that riding, but in an urban riding a great many patients in a hospital would ordinarily reside outside that riding.
For a moment I had thought the hon. member for Regina City was going to bring forth the argument that because university students are permitted to vote at their university, then perhaps patients in a hospital should be allowed to vote in the constituency where the hospital was situated. Had he gone that far there certainly would have been a presumption of reasonableness. I may say this is the first time the proposal has occurred to me but as he did not pursue it any further I shall not deal with it because, to be truthful, I do not know if I have a substantial argument. However, in a large hospital in a municipal area, with 500 patients, it is probable that not more than 50 or 60, possibly 100, would actually be resident in the constituency where the hospital is located. It seems to me more desirable that the majority of the patients should be enfranchised by having machinery whereby they could vote

in their own constituencies. In saying this, again I come back to the suggestion of a permanent voters list and absentee voting.
I do not wish to talk about that particular proposal at this time because it is not directly contained in the motion before the house, but I do think the difficulties outlined by the hon. member for York-Scarborough present quite a problem.
To me the only solution seems to lie in a permanent voters list which, if it is to be successful, would involve participation by the federal and provincial authorities, which seems to be a very timely topic, and since we are discussing a great many other things concerning the federal government and the provincial governments then perhaps the laudable motives of the mover of the motion would be fulfilled through a permanent voters list. Not only would that solve the problem of hospital patients, but it would also help those classes mentioned by the hon. member for Regina City.
I think all hon. members have had dealings with electors who feel they have been unjustly deprived of their right to vote. It seems to me it is the desire of all of us to extend the franchise to the greatest number of people possible, and though a great deal of administrative difficulty may be involved, it seems to me that, collectively, the people who have responsibility in this field-and I include among them the members of the committee on privileges and elections-should have sufficient imagination and ability to devise a system whereby the right to vote is extended wherever practicable.
I am not only thinking of people in hospitals. In my own province of Newfoundland, many people engaged in the seasonal fishery find it necessary to move from one part of the island to another, and it is often the case that they find themselves disfranchised. At the present time the seal fishery is under way, and if an election were called many hundreds of people who have left their homes to go to the ice would be disfranchised. It seems to me we should tackle this question on a broader basis so as to deal not only with the case of those confined in hospitals but also with these other cases to which I have referred, as well as those which have been mentioned by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz), the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More) and others who have spoken.
It is certainly my hope that the subject matter of this motion will be referred to the committee on privileges and elections. I trust this committee will shortly be constituted, because there is a good chance of continuity in its membership; a number of members who have already served on that committee would

be available to sit on it again. I am sure they have the imagination and the ability to resolve some of these difficulties, and I feel this would be an appropriate occasion on which to do so.

subtopic: VOTING PRIVILEGES FOR PATIENTS IN PUBLIC HOSPITALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say just a few words on the hon. member's motion. I am certain that he introduced it in good faith, and I, for my part, believe that those sick people have a valid reason for not voting. We should therefore, accept it.
Why worry because an infinitesimal part of people, perhaps once in their lifetime, have to forgo their right to vote?
No, Mr. Speaker. To my mind we should rather worry about the very large number of people who are able to do their duty and vote, but stay away from the polls.
That is the alarming aspect, and not the case of a few voters who happen to be in hospital at the time. Illness is a thing that does happen to several people, during an election, and I might well be hospitalized myself and lose my right to vote. That is hardly a catastrophe, in so far as it happens only once.
Rather than amend the Canada Elections Act on such a flimsy point, we should proceed with a few much more urgent changes. If the hon. member has gained some experience in several elections, he should be familiar with the complications arising from those transfers in a riding, more particularly in the last days before an election.
If the Canada Elections Act is ever amended with regard to travelling polls, it should not only extend to hospitals, but to all people having to stay at home because of invalidity or other ailments.

I should like to commend the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. McNulty) for having introduced this notice of motion. I have served as a returning officer and I know what it is like to face disgruntled people who have not been allowed to exercise their franchise.

These are the people who have moved their place of residence between the date of the issue of the writ and the date of the election. If they have not moved very far it is possible for them to get back to the riding where they are registered so as to exercise their franchise. A man might be able to get back himself, if the distance was not too great, but he could not very well take his family back to vote.
Inquiries of the Ministry
How could this difficulty be resolved? Application might be made to a returning officer who would be in a position, if the legislation were changed, to issue a certificate to provide that the elector's name be removed from the list in his old riding and sent to the returning officer in the area to which he has moved, where it could be added to the list. As I was saying, I do not propose to extend these remarks. Indeed, if I had not been stopped, I might possibly have finished by this time, but I will say to the committee and the minister that this question of a constitutional bill of rights for the protection of the fundamental rights of citizens, in my opinion is an important responsibility of his department.
While I recognize that the minister has only recently assumed his responsibilities, I hope that when his next estimates are presented he will be able to say something very definite about this matter. What I am saying today is that we, in this corner of the house at least, are serving notice that we expect some action from him in this regard.
I was pointing out the weaknesses of the existing bill of rights as passed by this parliament, and saying that one of its weaknesses is that it has no effect on provincial legislation which has constituted the main threat to civil liberties, with the exception, perhaps, of the Japanese Canadians, with which I was very familiar. With that single exception the invasions of civil liberties by provincial governments and legislatures has been more frequent. I am not going to cite them all now.

Supply-Justice
There was the press act of Alberta, the padlock act in the province of Quebec, and the acts of the legislatures of Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island that restricted freedom of association.
There has also been the recent act of the legislature of British Columbia that interfered with the rights of trade unions to contribute to election campaigns, and we have had a situation where the cabinet of the province of Ontario brought forward legislation that has justly been described by the press as the most offensive and dangerous legislation ever introduced in that province. It was described, by the ill-fated introducer of it as, "drastic, dangerous, new and terrible."
We all know that a vigilant press, an aroused public and a determined opposition secured the withdrawal of that legislation, but what I am trying to point out is that the bill of rights had no application to that threat, and apparently had no educative effect on the members of the Ontario government who sponsored the legislation. Even in respect to legislation passed by this parliament, a series of decisions has made it clear that the bill of rights is ineffective as its general language gives way to specific legislation inconsistent with it.
What I suggest is needed, and I recommend this to the Minister of Justice, is the incorporation in the constitution, and binding on parliament and the legislatures of a clear statement of fundamental principles setting out the basic liberties of the subject. I think one of the primary duties of the department is the considering of the constitutional structure of Canada as a whole, and also giving a lead to securing such a fundamental bill of rights as I have mentioned. Then there would be no danger of provincial or federal invasion of this particular field.
This would of course involve consultation with the provinces, and will also involve consultation with other experts in the field. More than a month ago I put a question on the order paper to the minister, question No. 229, which has remained unanswered. It was in respect to this very matter.
The whole problem of federal-provincial relations which is concerning all thoughtful Canadians can best be resolved, I suggest, in the context of effective federal leadership in the field of a new declaration of fundamental principles upon which the whole Canadian compact and constitution is based.
Before I sit down I want to refer to just one other aspect of individual rights which I suggest is urgently needed, and I merely suggest it for consideration. It is the question of a proper system of criminal legal aid. I have had, and no doubt the minister has had,

many briefs on this subject. As a matter of fact some of the best briefs I received were from the John Howard Society of B.C., and the B.C. civil liberties association. I do not propose to read this at length, but the brief of the John Howard Society of B.C. points out that our Criminal Code provides that a person is entitled in a criminal case "to make full answer and defence personally, or by counsel," and the bill of rights provides for a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice. These declarations which are in important statutes of this parliament, the Criminal Code and the bill of rights, require a fair hearing and evidence that a person should be able to make answer to criminal charges. But can a trial be fair and fundamentally just when an accused person attempts to defend himself without counsel?
That question has been dealt with by the United States supreme court. I shall not quote its judgment at length, but as recently as 1963 that court said:
... Reason and reflection require us to recognize that in our adversary system of criminal justice, any person haled into court, who is too poor to hire a lawyer, cannot be assured a fair trial unless counsel is provided for him.
That seems to be an obvious truth. I point out that the crown provides for the prosecution of those charged with offences in order to protect the fundamental rights of the public, but the fundamental rights of the accused cannot be forgotten.
The minister may say that this is essentially a matter for the provinces but I suggest that section 91 (27) of the British North America Act gives responsibility to the federal parliament in criminal procedure, and thus indicates that the federal parliament must take a lead in this field. I know many provinces are seeking to develop adequate systems of legal aid and I suggest this is a field for co-operative federalism. One of the responsibilities of the minister should be to call together those who represent the provinces in this field and work out a fully satisfactory means of providing legal aid, which in the United States is said to be a high constitutional right of every individual accused. This is something which should also be developed in Canada. The rights of people accused in Canada should be no less than the rights of people accused in the United States.
These are the two subjects, that of a constitutional amendment to make an effective bill of rights, and criminal legal aid, which I respectfully suggest to the minister could be receiving his earnest attention. I do not expect him to answer these questions now, but I do serve notice on him that we will

look to him for a real lead in this field. For far too long the Department of Justice has been a department which has, no doubt, provided useful services to the government and to the country, but I think it has done all too little to blaze a trail in the development of the civil rights and liberties of all Canadians. I hope that under the leadership of the present minister the situation will change, and I serve notice on him that we shall continue to draw these matters to his attention.

Some people may say this is only a small matter, Mr. Chairman, but I believe it is a matter of the kind which backbenchers must regard with a special concern. A gentleman in my constituency who is a war veteran- he had a very good record in the second world war-holds a licence as a plumber. I do not imagine that anybody, by any stretch of the imagination could declare that a plumber in a penitentiary was carrying out a custodial function. The maximum age for this position is 45, and you are 48 years old.
