Order. Since the hon. member has now expressed his opinion and made his representations, I may take this opportunity to make a ruling on the point of order raised a while ago by the Minister of Justice.
Of course, I feel sure that the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue has realized the soundness of the point raised by the minister in the sense-
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue will let me conclude my remarks. -In the sense that we cannot anticipate an order of the house, in the case pointed out by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue, who himself admitted that he had to limit his observations, in a certain measure, in view of the fact that there was already an order of the house on the same matter.
In the case that has just been raised by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, we are faced with the same difficulty. There is at least one bill, namely Bill C-19, which is now listed on the order paper of the house. In the circumstances, hon. members are not entitled to enter into a debate with respect to that matter.

Mr. Chairman, in that case, I shall raise another point.
I know that the government intends to appoint a judge who will be in charge of divorce cases for the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland.
May I ask the Minister of Justice whether he intends to consult not only the civic authorities but also the religious authorities in the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland, because I do not believe that it is possible, under the constitution, to impose on the provinces concerned something they probably do not want, without consulting them and obtaining their assent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, of course, the legislative measure mentioned by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm is not aimed at setting up divorce courts for the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland.
I do not want to say much about it, because it is now on the order paper and will be discussed as soon as the order of the day is called. But nevertheless, it is indeed an act for the sole purpose of investing upon a judge the powers of a divorce commissioner, a position which was established by the house during the last session.
However, I think that when the bill in question receives second reading, I shall have the opportunity of explaining to the house what it is all about and the nature of the powers that this legislative measure will confer on an additional judge of the exchequer court.

Mr. Chairman, since this is another bill before the house and I cannot speak about it, just as in the case of sweepstakes, I shall try once again to deal with a subject which does not concern any bill now before this house, which will permit me to make my observations while conforming to your requirements.
Recently, the chiefs of police of Canada held a convention during which certain films shown over the television networks, particularly the C.B.C., were strongly criticized.
The Canadian chiefs of police association has submitted a brief to the Minister of Justice-when the former minister of justice was head of the department-asking him to find some way, not to impose people on the C.B.C., but rather to exert more pressure so that the C.B.C. itself might select a special committee made up, for instance, of educators, parents and religious authorities, in order to exercise some supervision on films shown on television, especially those shown at the time young people settle down before their television sets.
Police chiefs in Canada were unanimous to state that one of the main causes of crime
Supply-Justice
and juvenile delinquency in general throughout Canada was the showing of movies exploiting crime, sex, and passion on television at hours when young people are among the viewers.
Without alluding to anybody in the C.B.C., I would ask the minister whether it would be possible to find a practical way so that T.V. networks, such as the C.B.C. itself, might set up an organization to supervise the movies shown at hours when young people are listening.
Because he received many letters from all over the country, from authorities of all religious denominations, educators and parents, the minister must be aware of the general concern over the freedom taken in that respect by the C.B.C. national television network which is financed by taxpayers throughout Canada.
Consequently, I would ask the minister whether it would not be possible to find, in consultation with the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne), a compromise which would enable the C.B.C. to recommend to the government the establishment of such a committee and to act upon the representations made by parents, educators, religious authorities, and also by the chiefs of police at their recent convention.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to labour that point too long either, but I wish to say that I have inherited from my predecessor, as suggested by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, the very policy concerning the association to which he referred earlier.
Mr. Chairman, for reasons which can be readily understood, I have not yet had the opportunity of considering to my satisfaction the problem and of establishing definitely under whose jurisdiction this whole matter comes nor the solutions likely to be brought forward. The problem can obviously be considered from many angles. First, the viewpoint of Canadians and parents who have to exercise their authority on their children; second, the time at which the programs are shown; third, the question of censorship and liberty of television; fourth, should the state-owned network be treated differently from privately-owned networks.
I can assure my hon. friend that as a citizen of this country and as a father, I am very much interested in this problem and that I shall do my utmost to discuss this matter with my colleagues.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask a
supplementary question?
Does the minister consider that each province could use its own censorship organization to supervise programs or films presented

Supply-Justice
on the television networks? The province of Quebec has its own censorship organization; is the minister not of the opinion that this comes under provincial jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I realize that all questions ought to be answered, provided they are in order according to our rules and regulations. But I feel sure that my hon. friend is now asking me for an opinion on a constitutional matter that I have no right to give to the house.
All I can say is that, when I was teaching law, that was a question I liked to ask the people in my class and they did not always come up with a perfect answer, in the sense suggested by my hon. friend. I feel it is premature to discuss it here, for this is not the right moment for that. Furthermore, the question is purely theoretical, since it is meant to determine whether or not such an act, if it were passed by the provinces, would be constitutional. But, to the extent that the matter falls within the scope of the question, I promised to take it into serious consideration, and I shall do so.

Mr. Chairman, before the item is passed I know that the minister wants to answer the question asked by my hon. friend from Pontiac-Temiscamingue on the constitutionality of section 3 of the bill concerning the Canada pension plan.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think that the hon. member for Three Rivers was not in the house when that point was raised by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue, but a question was asked and an answer given by the Minister of Justice, and we agreed that such matters were not in order and should be discussed some other time.
Mr. Chairman, with all due respect, the question was in order and I thought that the minister was ready to give me an answer, but later on I did not get any.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Peace River. Is the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue raising a point of order?

I have no wish to interrupt my hon. friend, but before going on to another item, even if it is in order, I think that the minister should give us some explanations. After all, he comes to the house to have some votes passed, and the least he could do is answer the questions put to him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the question has already been answered, though perhaps not to the satisfaction of the hon. member, but I think that under standing orders, the substance of the question raised is irregular because it tends to prolong the debate.
There is no question of drawing out the debate; the minister has only to answer yes or no.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have here a quite important question of policy and, even if we were discussing the first item in the main budget, I think that it is not up to me to answer a question specifically asked by my hon. friend from Pontiac-Temiscamingue because, according to the functions he has assumed, the Minister of Justice is the adviser of the crown in all constitutional matters.
It is therefore obvious that the same pretext might be used to raise questions with regard to the constitutional character of every statute, every clause and every item before us, and, for purely mathematical reasons, it would be an endless procedure. It seems to me that the discussion will be much more in order when the bill presented by the Minister of National Health and Welfare comes up for second reading.

Mr. Chairman, in June, 1963, I asked the minister at that time a question with regard to the matter of the legality of the means proposed by the government in making a change of administrative responsibility for the Eskimos in northern Quebec. On June 28 I asked him this question dealing with the transfer of responsibility for the Eskimos:
If any such agreement is reached, will it be submitted to parliament?
The minister then said the question was a hypothetical one and did not answer it. Since that time I have posed the question a number of times, as have other hon. members. It has now been admitted that an agreement of sorts has been reached between Canada and Quebec and I think this is an excellent time for the minister, sitting here not only in his capacity as Minister of Justice in respect of whose estimates we are now having a discussion but also, of course, as one of the ministers dealing with the question of this particular transfer, to answer this question. I make this very definite statement, Mr. Chairman, that as I understand it, the method which the government proposes to use is completely unconstitutional and should not be permitted. I want to illustrate this very briefly and put these points before the committee at this time. As has been admitted Canada secured, after trying to evade it, responsibility in 1939 as a result of a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada. In the result the court answered a very simple question. The question was:	Are Eskimos of
northern Quebec Indians within the meaning of term 24 of the British North America Act,

section 91? The answer was very simply: Yes, they are. This was the entire answer made by the Supreme Court of Canada. This being the case, by section 91 Canada has exclusive jurisdiction; but not the government of Canada, the parliament of Canada. I think-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I have some doubt as to whether the point raised by the hon. member falls within the ambit of the resolution now before the committee. Perhaps the hon. member might enlighten the Chair as to how this relates specifically to the item before us.

Mr. Chairman, this matter turns on a question of the constitutionality of a step which is to be taken in connection with the transfer of responsibility for certain Canadian people for whom this parliament is responsible. It has been admitted in the house that this transfer is going to take place. I am suggesting that the method by which it is to take place is unconstitutional. In my view the Minister of Justice, as attorney general, chief law officer of the crown and adviser to the cabinet, is now answering for his estimates and is in the position where he should be prepared to hear argument that this is not a constitutional process which the government proposes to take.
I am basing my view, Mr. Chairman, on the fact that we have agreed indirectly that there shall be general discussion, which normally possibly would not take place but because of the desire to push through interim supply this general understanding was reached. As a matter of fact, just to illustrate my point, I had prepared myself to and wished to discuss this particular issue on interim supply, but I yielded to the request of the government and did not do so. Now the estimates of the Minister of Justice are before the committee and this issue I am dealing with involves the constitutionality of a very grave and important proposal that the government has made. I am submitting that the way they intend to do it is unconstitutional and I think the minister is the proper person to entertain this argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? He made the statement that it had been admitted in the house that a transfer was to be made. Would he refer me to the quotation in Hansard where that statement was made?
I am sure my seatmate will be glad to look that up while I am proceeding with my argument.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a weak response.

It was during the course of a discussion when the Prime Minister, as I
Supply-Justice
recall, made the statement that before the transfer was made there would be consultation with the Eskimos.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The point I had in mind was that even though we are having a general discussion that discussion should relate to matters which affect the administration of the Department of Justice. The point being raised by the hon. member is very similar to others raised previously by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue and the hon. member for Three Rivers. In each case there is anticipation of legislation which may or may not come before the house. Perhaps there is not this difficulty in the case of the hon. member, but to my mind the discussion which he is starting now relates more closely to the administration of northern affairs than the Department of Justice. I wonder whether the hon. member has taken that into account?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. May I say that if there were legislation dealing with this matter on the order paper I would not need to say anything. I would not be making this argument; I would not be speaking. What we are complaining about is that there is no legislation when there should be. That is germane to my complaint. There is no legislation. What I submit is proposed to be done here is proposed to be done, if it is going to be done at all, by order in council, which I submit is completely unconstitutional, completely improper. That is the point of my argument. There is no legislation before us at all. I suggest that the Minister of Justice has an explanation to make here.
I will not be very long. I should like to make these points to illustrate my reason for suggesting that what is proposed is unconstitutional. The minister may be able to satisfy my anxiety on this score. If he can I will be very happy indeed. I was pointing out that the 1939 case vested jurisdiction over the Eskimos of northern Quebec in parliament and not in the hands of the government. Surely it has been settled many years ago that the legislative branch is supreme and that the government only has such power as parliament chooses to give to it. Until the Minister of Justice or the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is in a position to indicate to the house that the government has jurisdiction to make this transfer, then I suggest there is no way it can be done save by legislation.
I will complete my very brief argument on this point and then sit down and hope that the minister may answer me. I recall that when my colleague spoke on this matter on an interim supply bill he indicated that the government should bring in legislation and

Supply-Justice
then made the point that the effect of a statement made by the parliamentary secretary appeared to negative the suggestion and to indicate that legislation would not be brought in to implement the proposal.
I submit that if you examine section 91 of the British North America Act, Mr. Chairman, you will see the impropriety of what the government proposes to do. Without securing an act of parliament it is going to transfer jurisdiction by administrative process to a province. As far as that aspect is concerned, let me say that I make no objection to the fact that it might be eminently desirable in the long run for changes of jurisdiction of this kind to take place. This is not my argument. I am concerned with the manner in which it is proposed to be done. The government proposes to do it by means other than legislation. Let us consider what may be involved here-the health, education, welfare, the method by which property descends, devolution of estates and so on, relating to these Eskimos.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I raise a point of order which I will not press too hard, but because the supplementary estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources will be coming up at any moment now, I suggest very respectfully that item 1 of the estimates of the Department of Justice is hardly the place for this discussion. However, inasmuch as the hon. member has already gone quite far in asserting his very interesting position, I suggest that he be allowed to proceed even on my estimates but that we be allowed to answer this part of his speech when the northern affairs estimates are called.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think this is a very reasonable position. Actually it is the position that the Chair adopted in the case of the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue who was allowed to complete his argument, although perhaps he did not have as much time to do so as the hon. member for Peace River. I feel that the committee of supply is not the place to get an opinion from the Minister of Justice on the constitutionality of a statute. However, as the Minister of Justice is willing to listen to the point of view being expressed by the hon. member for Peace River I feel he should be allowed to complete his argument.

On the point of order.

On your point of order, Mr. Chairman, I must say that this discussion is quite relevant, since the Minister of Justice himself took part

in the discussions regarding the matter raised by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin).

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think his participation was to the extent of saying he should not be required to give an opinion.

Mr. Chairman, this is one of those famous compromises by which democracy works, though sometimes at greater length than it normally would. This is my submission. If I am correct in the assumption I have made from all of the questions and answers and what has been said on the subject, that it is the intention of the government to call this change an administrative change only and work it out by order in council without coming to parliament, then I submit this procedure is unconstitutional. I was making the point as to precisely what would be involved in these changes. They may call it administrative detail, but in fact it involves everything concerning the lives and the fortunes of 2,500 Canadians. True, there may be left in the hands of the federal government the empty shell of jurisdiction but active participation in all matters affecting these people will be in the hands of a provincial government.
If this is the position, what is going to happen to federal-provincial government responsibilities under sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act, that is if the federal government is going to follow the policy of making constitutional changes by order in council, rather than coming to parliament?
If this is the position, why is it not possible for them also by order in council to authorize a provincial government to issue a charter to a company to build a pipe line in order to permit that company to go to the national energy board? Why is it not possible for the government, upon the same basis of reasoning to give a provincial government authority, such as Mr. Bennett's government in British Columbia, by order in council and despite the provisions of section 91 of the British North America Act, to grant a charter to a group of people in British Columbia to operate a chartered bank? Why is it not possible, on the same basis of reasoning for the federal government, not parliament, to give to any other province authorization to raise its own army, and do it by means of order in council? This is precisely the basis of reasoning on which the government is now operating in their announced intention to proceed to make this constitutional change without coming to parliament. Parliament has exclusive jurisdiction. I use the word "parliament" as distinct from government. Parliament has exclusive

jurisdiction with regard to Indians, and this includes the Eskimos of northern Quebec. Until parliament has given the government the right to give to a provincial government any of its responsibilities in respect of these Indians, then the action which the government proposes to take is completely unconstitutional and not within the purview of the government as opposed to parliament. This is the simple issue I raise, and I think it deserves an answer.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. The minister, as he pointed out a while ago, had an opportunity to practise and teach law in the province of Quebec. He was in a position to be personally aware, as I am also, of the delays caused in that province by the rather large number of cases cluttering up the roll of the superior court. Therefore, does he intend to appoint enough new judges to meet the needs of the people, thereby providing for the smooth administration of justice in that province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am aware of that situation. I know that the roll of some of the courts of my province are overcrowded and I also know that this causes delays. I must explain how vacancies are filled in the superior court. There are two jurisdictions in the provinces which see to the establishment of courts, as well as to the appointment of a certain number of judges for a particular court. Once the province has set the number of judges for appointment to a court, it is under the Canadian constitution that the federal government must fill the new vacancies and appoint those judges.
I have just received a communication from the chief justice of the province of Quebec who is at present discussing the situation with the attorney general of that province. If ther are no further developments, the whole matter will rest with the province and we shall not interfere.
As far as the appointment of any judge is concerned, both federal and provincial statutes must be considered.

I should like to put another question to the Minister of Justice. Does the minister also intend to see that judges of the appeal court and of the supreme court, are in sufficient numbers to meet the requirements of justice in our province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
In the case of the supreme court, and the exchequer court, this matter, of course, comes under federal jurisdiction. But to my knowledge, no complaint has been received to the effect that the number of judges in those two courts is insufficient.
Supply-Justice
Mention was made earlier to a bill now on the order paper and tending to increase the number of judges in the exchequer court for a specific purpose, that is to grant powers to the commissioner for divorces. I am not aware of any complaint to the effect that there are not enough judges in the exchequer or in the Supreme Court of Canada or that there is any backlog in those courts.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the Minister of Justice a few questions regarding the construction of a penal institution in my riding, more especially in St. Pie de Bagot. I should like to know what reasons led his department and that of public works to cancel the decision previously taken to build a medium security prison in my riding, and especially in St. Pie de Bagot.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as far as I know, that matter was settled before I took over as Minister of Justice. I do not think I can say anything more at this time. It might be possible to discuss this further when my department main estimates are considered.
I am not fully informed of the reasons which led to the decision reached in that case. I can say, however, that they are the same reasons which caused my predecessor to uphold, for instance, the decision he took in the case of Drumheller after extensive consultations. It would be neither honest nor realistic to go further than this. I readily admit that I am not aware enough of the facts referred to by the hon. member to give a complete and satisfactory answer.

The minister could merely ask the necessary information of his parliamentary secretary (Mr. Macdonald) who is beside him at the present time. Indeed, I myself could, I think, inform the minister. But before going any further, I would like also to ask the minister whether he has considered taking the necessary decisions to make good the great injustice committed by his predecessor concerning the riding of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot. Since the minister does not seem to have enough information to give a reply, I could make a summary of what happened at the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary but I shall just say that we have here a shameful example of patronage on the part of the present government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I do not think it is permissible for an hon. member to make, on supplementary estimates, such unfounded accusations concerning recent events about which I am not sufficiently informed to make comments, as the hon. member is fully aware. Furthermore, those remarks are hardly relevant to vote No. le which provides for

Royal Assent
the approval of an expenditure of $10,000 to pay for the expenses of the international criminological congress which will be held in Canada in 1965.

Mr. Chairman, I have a lot of respect and admiration for the Minister of Justice. However, I do not think I have to accept the directives he wants to give me. I have before me all I need to prove to the Minister of Justice that it is not an unfounded charge, but facts which speak eloquently for the action taken by the Liberal party and the present government. I will certainly not miss this opportunity to put before the house and the country the true facts so that the people of my riding in particular, those of Quebec and Canada as a whole may know how much the present government has indulged in smalltime patronage.
In 1958, Mr, Chairman, the Department of Justice was planning to get new prison facilities because St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary had become too small. Therefore, at that time, I took steps to find, together with employees of the Department of Public Works and the Department of Justice, the lands necessary for the construction of a medium security penitentiary in my constituency. This institution was going to cost about $4,500,000 to build, and the work would allow the hiring in my constituency, of a good many people, about 200 heads of families. As you may well imagine, the citizens of my constituency learned with satisfaction that the then minister of justice, Mr. Davie Fulton, had decided to grant to that part of the country, a penal institution which would have brought great prosperity first to the town of St. Pie, and second, to the whole St. Hya-cinthe area.
Mr. Chairman, it is now a quarter to ten and I see that the President of the Privy Council wishes to be recognized.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I want to thank the hon. member for yielding me the floor. We are expecting momentarily a message from the other place for royal assent at a quarter to ten, and I wonder whether in the circumstances it would be more appropriate for us to rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again at the next sitting of the house?

Agreed.
Progress reported.

I have the honour to inform the house that I have received the following communication:
Government House, Ottawa, April 1964.
Sir:
X have the honour to inform you that the Honourable Robert Taschereau, P.C., Chief Justice of Canada, acting as Deputy of His Excellency the Governor General, will proceed to the Senate chamber today, the 6th of April, at 9.45 p.m., for the purpose of giving the royal assent to certain bills.
I have the honour to be, sir.
Your obedient servant,
A. G. Cherrier,
Assistant Secretary to the Governor General.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I would ask the house leader if he will announce the business for tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we will proceed with the balance, I hope, of the supplementary estimates, after which the rest of the time during the day will be used for the debate on the second reading of the Canada pension plan bill, and the next first full two days will be taken to conclude the debate on the budget.
May I ask the house leader when it is his intention to establish the standing committees?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that it is the intention of the government to establish the standing committees right away. It is a matter of mechanics, getting the steering committee together to provide the names for the various parties. The proportion of the members on the various committees has been worked out already.

A message was delivered by Major C. R. Lamoureux, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the honourable the Deputy Governor General desires the immediate attendance of this honourable house in the chamber of the honourable the Senate.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker with the house went up to the Senate chamber.
And being returned:
Mr. Speaker informed the house that the Deputy Governor General had been pleased to give, in Her Majesty's name, the royal assent of the following bill:
An act for granting to Her Majesty certain sums of money for the public service for the financial year ending the 31st March, 1964.
It being eight minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put.
Tuesday, April 7, 1964
